- [concept] The Gateway protocol documents requests sent by Claude Code to a gateway, including required forwarding fields and features that stop working if those fields are stripped. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol
- [fact] A running Claude apps gateway serves a machine-readable version of this contract at the GET /protocol endpoint. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol
- [concept] The Gateway protocol includes forwarding requirements plus Claude apps gateway-specific endpoints for SSO sign-in, managed-settings delivery, and telemetry. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol
- [fact] Claude apps gateway runs from the same claude binary as the CLI. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol
- [actionable] Use the Claude apps gateway quickstart to obtain a running instance for fetching the protocol spec. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol
- [concept] The Gateway protocol uses two terms for how a gateway handles headers and body fields: 'Forward unchanged' and 'Consume'. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol
- [fact] 'Forward unchanged' means passing the field to the upstream byte-for-byte. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol
- [concept] 'Consume' means the gateway may read the field for routing, attribution, or tracing and need not forward it. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol
- [fact] Any field not marked 'forward unchanged' is optional for the gateway to consume or ignore. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol
- [concept] A gateway must expose at least one API format to Claude Code clients, and the client selects the format using specific variables. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [fact] Google Cloud's Agent Platform is Google Cloud's Claude endpoint, formerly Vertex AI, and its variable names retain the `VERTEX` spelling. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [concept] Microsoft Foundry and the Claude Platform on AWS implement the Anthropic Messages format. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [fact] A gateway fronting the Claude Platform on AWS must forward the `anthropic-workspace-id` header on every request. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [fact] Token-counting endpoints are optional; when absent, Claude Code falls back to counting context usage through the inference endpoint. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [fact] Inference requests post to `/v1/messages?beta=true`, so matching should be done on the path rather than the full URL. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [fact] Google Cloud's Agent Platform method suffixes attach to the publisher model path, as in `/projects/{project}/locations/{location}/publishers/anthropic/models/{model}:streamRawPredict`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [concept] Gateways receive best-effort startup traffic that can be rejected without breaking functionality. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [fact] An Anthropic Messages-format gateway receives a `HEAD /api/hello` connection-warming probe, which Claude Code skips when an HTTP proxy or client certificate is configured. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [fact] An Amazon Bedrock-format gateway receives a `GET /inference-profiles?type=SYSTEM_DEFINED` request and, for inference profiles, `GET /inference-profiles/{profile}` lookups. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [problem] The fast mode availability check never appears in gateway logs because it calls `api.anthropic.com` directly rather than following `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [fact] The WebFetch domain safety check also calls `api.anthropic.com` directly. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [concept] Inference responses must stream; buffering complete responses before relaying them stalls the client. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [fact] On connections through `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` or `ANTHROPIC_AWS_BASE_URL`, Claude Code counts every byte relayed, including SSE `ping` events and comment lines. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [problem] Claude Code aborts a stream that goes silent for 300 seconds by default on `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` or `ANTHROPIC_AWS_BASE_URL` connections. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [actionable] When translating from an upstream that sends no pings (like Amazon Bedrock's binary event-stream), emit your own `ping` events during silent gaps. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [fact] Gateways reached through `ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_BASE_URL`, `ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_BASE_URL`, or `ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_BASE_URL` are not wrapped by the byte-level watchdog, even when relaying Anthropic Messages format. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [fact] On `ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_BASE_URL` connections, a 5-minute idle timeout aborts a silent stream instead of the byte watchdog. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [actionable] Add the byte watchdog on `ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_BASE_URL` connections by setting the `CLAUDE_ENABLE_BYTE_WATCHDOG_BEDROCK` environment variable. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [problem] A common failure mode is a mismatch between the format the client sends to the gateway and the format the upstream provider accepts. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [fact] When the client speaks Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud's Agent Platform format, Claude Code sends only the subset of capabilities those providers accept. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [fact] When the client speaks Anthropic Messages format, Claude Code sends the full set of capabilities even if forwarding to Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud's Agent Platform upstreams. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#api-formats
- [concept] Claude Code prepends an attribution block to the system prompt containing the client version and a conversation fingerprint. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#system-prompt-attribution-block
- [fact] The `api.anthropic.com` endpoint strips the attribution block before processing when it arrives unchanged as the first system block, preserving first-party prompt caching. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#system-prompt-attribution-block
- [problem] If a gateway reshapes the `system` array by prepending blocks, reordering, or converting to a single string, the attribution strip fails and the block reaches the model and cache key. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#system-prompt-attribution-block
- [problem] Merging the attribution header into another system block causes the endpoint to drop the entire merged entry, including the rest of the system prompt. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#system-prompt-attribution-block
- [actionable] Set `CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0` in the environment to omit the attribution block entirely if the gateway must reshape system content. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#system-prompt-attribution-block
- [idea] Omit the attribution block at the client level rather than stripping or moving it in the gateway, as Anthropic and cloud providers read the block for attribution. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#system-prompt-attribution-block
- [fact] Claude Code keeps the attribution block on auto mode classifier requests even when `CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0` is set if requests go to `api.anthropic.com` with no third-party provider and no profile/federation credential. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#system-prompt-attribution-block
- [fact] When routing through an LLM gateway, using a third-party provider, or with a profile/federation credential active, setting `CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0` removes the block from classifier requests. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#system-prompt-attribution-block
- [problem] Before v2.1.229, setting `CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0` removed the block from classifier requests, causing auto mode to fail on every action when the API declined unidentified requests. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#system-prompt-attribution-block
- [fact] From Claude Code v2.1.181, the attribution block is stable for the lifetime of a conversation when requests route through a custom base URL. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#system-prompt-attribution-block
- [idea] When using a gateway that implements prompt caching keyed on the request body or forwards to third-party providers like Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, or Google Cloud's Agent Platform, set `CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#system-prompt-attribution-block
- [problem] Before v2.1.181, the attribution block included a per-request token that changed the start of the system prompt on every request, reducing prompt-cache reuse on third-party providers. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol#system-prompt-attribution-block

- [problem] A `404` response indicates the model name is not routed at the gateway, while a `401` from the provider suggests the gateway's provider credential is incorrect. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-rollout#rollout-steps
- [problem] Serving the gateway behind a redirect can drop the request body or strip the credential header, causing model discovery to fail. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-rollout#rollout-steps

- [definition] Choose a pattern — Claude Code supports a range of restriction levels. - [definition] Exclusive control with managed-mcp.json — If you deploy a `managed-mcp.json` file, Claude Code loads only the servers that file defines, plus any in-process servers the app that started the session registers, such as the VS Code extension's own server or the [connectors the desktop app… — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [definition] Authenticate with per-user credentials — Any user on the machine can read this file, so don't store API keys or other credentials in `env` blocks. Pass per-user credentials with one of these instead: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#authenticate-with-per-user-credentials
- [definition] Validate the configuration — To confirm the file is in effect, run two checks on a managed machine: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#validate-the-configuration
- [definition] Disable MCP entirely — Deploy a `managed-mcp.json` containing an empty server map to block every MCP server apart from [in-process servers the app that started the session registers](#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcp-json): — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#disable-mcp-entirely
- [definition] Allow claude.ai connectors alongside the managed set — By default, deploying `managed-mcp.json` suppresses the [claude.ai connectors](/docs/en/mcp#use-mcp-servers-from-claude-ai) Claude Code fetches itself, including connectors an administrator configured for the organization in the claude.ai admin console. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#allow-claudeai-connectors-alongside-the-managed-set
- [definition] Policy-based control with allowlists and denylists — Allowlists and denylists filter which configured servers are allowed to load. They aren't a registry: a server still has to be added by a user, a plugin, or `managed-mcp.json` before the allowlist or denylist applies to it. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#policy-based-control-with-allowlists-and-denylists
- [definition] Match servers by URL, command, or name — `allowedMcpServers` and `deniedMcpServers` are lists of entries. Each entry is an object with a single key that identifies servers by their URL, their command, or their name: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#match-servers-by-url-command-or-name
- [definition] How a server is evaluated — Before loading a server, including one from `managed-mcp.json`, Claude Code runs the three checks below in order. - [definition] Example configuration — The configuration below sets up a hard allowlist with a denylist. The highlighted lines change how the rest of the list is evaluated, and the callouts after the block explain each one: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#example-configuration

- [definition] Configuration summary — Every file and setting this page covers, what it controls, and how to deliver it: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#configuration-summary
- [concept] Claude Code supports restriction levels using managed-mcp.json for fixed sets or allowedMcpServers/deniedMcpServers for filtering user configurations. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#choose-a-pattern
- [fact] Claude Code does not have a built-in MCP server registry that users can browse and install from. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#choose-a-pattern
- [idea] For the approved-catalog pattern, share the approved list and its claude mcp add commands on an internal wiki or distribute servers as plugins through a managed plugin marketplace. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#choose-a-pattern
- [concept] Deploying a managed-mcp.json file grants exclusive control, loading only defined servers plus in-process ones while blocking all others. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [fact] Users cannot add, modify, or use any other MCP servers, including plugin-provided servers and those passed via the --mcp-config CLI flag. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [problem] On a workstation, passing --mcp-config when an enterprise config is present causes Claude Code to exit with: You cannot dynamically configure MCP servers when an enterprise MCP config is present. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [fact] In cloud sessions on hosts where the file is deployed, Claude Code starts with managed servers only and skips claude.ai connectors delivered by the host. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [problem] Before version 2.1.229, cloud sessions with a managed config exited with the same error as workstations instead of starting silently. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [fact] Claude Code names skipped servers in a warning on stderr, which self-hosted runners record at the debug log level. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [problem] Passing --strict-mcp-config causes Claude Code to exit at startup on both workstations and cloud sessions because it attempts to replace the managed set. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [concept] The allowedMcpServers and deniedMcpServers settings apply to managed servers, filtering which ones load based on policy checks. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [fact] A user's own deniedMcpServers merges with the managed set, allowing users to block specific managed servers for themselves. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [fact] managed-mcp.json is a standalone file that cannot be delivered through server-managed settings and requires administrator privileges to deploy. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [idea] Deploy the file across a fleet using device management tools like Jamf, Group Policy, Intune, or custom Linux fleet management. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [fact] Claude Code looks for managed-mcp.json at specific system paths defined in the documentation. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [concept] The file uses the same format as a project .mcp.json file, defining servers via a JSON structure. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [problem] Do not store API keys or credentials in env blocks within managed-mcp.json because any user on the machine can read the file. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [idea] Pass per-user credentials using ${VAR} expansion, OAuth, per-user headers, or the headersHelper function instead of static secrets. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [actionable] Run claude mcp list to verify only servers in managed-mcp.json are loaded; if user servers appear, check the file path and permissions. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [problem] Running claude mcp add fails with Cannot add MCP server: enterprise MCP configuration is active and has exclusive control over MCP servers. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [actionable] Deploy a managed-mcp.json containing an empty server map to disable all MCP servers except in-process ones registered by the app. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [problem] When disabling MCP entirely, previously configured user servers stop loading on the next session start without any warning about the policy. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [concept] By default, deploying managed-mcp.json suppresses claude.ai connectors fetched by Claude Code, including those configured in the admin console. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [idea] Set allowAllClaudeAiMcps to true in a managed settings source to load claude.ai connectors alongside the managed set. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [fact] Allowlists and denylists still apply to claude.ai connectors even when allowAllClaudeAiMcps is enabled, allowing specific blocks via deniedMcpServers. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [problem] The allowAllClaudeAiMcps setting affects only connectors fetched by Claude Code; plugin-provided servers remain suppressed. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [problem] A managed-mcp.json on a cloud session host suppresses that session's connectors regardless of the allowAllClaudeAiMcps setting. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [fact] No managed-mcp.json file reaches the connectors delivered by the desktop app to its local and SSH sessions. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#exclusive-control-with-managed-mcpjson
- [concept] When managed-mcp.json is deployed alongside sessions with --mcp-config servers, the behavior depends on whether exclusive control is active. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#how-restrictions-appear-to-users
- [problem] If a server disappears due to policy restrictions, users receive no signal indicating that policy is the reason for the disappearance. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#how-restrictions-appear-to-users
- [actionable] When rolling out new restrictions, you must tell affected users which servers are blocked to compensate for the lack of user-facing signals. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#how-restrictions-appear-to-users
- [concept] When OpenTelemetry export is configured, Claude Code can record which MCP servers and tools users invoke. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#monitor-mcp-usage
- [actionable] Set `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1` to include MCP server and tool names in tool events. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#monitor-mcp-usage
- [fact] The full event schema for monitoring usage is available in the Monitoring documentation. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#monitor-mcp-usage

Every mechanism carries the same policy keys as a `settings.json` file, so the [settings reference](/docs/en/settings-reference) applies to all of them. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings#choose-a-delivery-mechanism
- [definition] Where and when a policy applies — A deployed policy reaches the developer's sessions as follows: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings#where-and-when-a-policy-applies
- [definition] Where each mechanism stores the policy — The keys are the same everywhere, but each mechanism stores them in a different place and shape: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings#where-each-mechanism-stores-the-policy
- [definition] Split a file-based policy across teams — If several teams own parts of one policy, put each part in its own file in `managed-settings.d/`, next to `managed-settings.json` in the same system directory, instead of editing one shared file. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings#split-a-file-based-policy-across-teams
- [definition] How Claude Code combines managed sources — When your organization delivers more than one managed source to the same machine, the [`managedSourcesBehavior`](/docs/en/settings-reference#managedsourcesbehavior) key decides what Claude Code does with the others: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings#how-claude-code-combines-managed-sources
- [definition] Keys read from every admin source — Under the default `"first-wins"` setting, Claude Code reads most keys only from the [source it selected](#how-claude-code-combines-managed-sources), and ignores a value in a lower-ranked source even when the selected source leaves that key unset. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings#keys-read-from-every-admin-source
- [definition] Compose every managed source — To have Claude Code apply every admin source your organization delivers, set [`managedSourcesBehavior`](/docs/en/settings-reference#managedsourcesbehavior) to `"merge"` in the highest-ranked source you deploy. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings#compose-every-managed-source
- [definition] Compute the policy with a helper program — A [`policyHelper`](/docs/en/settings-reference#policyhelper) is an executable your MDM policy or managed settings file names, and Claude Code runs it to compute managed settings at startup. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings#compute-the-policy-with-a-helper-program
- [definition] Let an embedding host add policy — When another application launches Claude Code, such as Claude Desktop, an IDE extension, or an Agent SDK app, that host can pass its own managed settings through the SDK `managedSettings` option. Claude Code calls these parent settings. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings#let-an-embedding-host-add-policy
- [definition] What a developer can change — A developer's own settings files, `--settings` values, and project files never override a managed value; the [exceptions](/docs/en/settings#exceptions-to-managed-settings-precedence) only let a stricter lower-level value count. Four things sit outside that rule: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings#what-a-developer-can-change
- [definition] Check that a policy is in force — A developer reports that a policy isn't applying, or you want to confirm a rollout landed before pushing it to the fleet. Two commands on that machine answer it: `/status` shows which managed source Claude Code selected, and `claude doctor` lists what it dropped. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings#check-that-a-policy-is-in-force
- [definition] Read the source in /status — On the developer's machine, run `/status` inside Claude Code and read the `Setting sources` line. When a managed source is in effect, the line lists `Enterprise managed settings` with the source Claude Code selected in parentheses: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings#read-the-source-in-status
- [definition] Find entries Claude Code dropped — When a managed settings file, MDM profile, registry value, or server-managed payload fails schema validation, Claude Code first skips the individual entries it can repair, such as one invalid permission rule, with a warning for each, then drops any top-level key whose value still fails and keeps… — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings#find-entries-claude-code-dropped
- [definition] Keys only a managed source can set — Claude Code reads the following keys only from a managed source; placing them in user or project settings files has no effect. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings#keys-only-a-managed-source-can-set
- [definition] Turn telemetry off for your organization — Claude Code sends Anthropic operational [telemetry](/docs/en/data-usage#telemetry-services) by default on sessions that use the Anthropic API, whether directly, through an LLM gateway, or through a custom `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`; [Default behaviors by API… — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings#turn-telemetry-off-for-your-organization

- [definition] Find and build MCP servers — Browse reviewed connectors in the [Anthropic Directory](https://claude.ai/directory). - [definition] Installing MCP servers — MCP servers can be configured in several ways depending on your needs: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#installing-mcp-servers
- [definition] Option 1: Add a remote HTTP server — HTTP servers are the recommended option for connecting to remote MCP servers. This is the most widely supported transport for cloud-based services. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#option-1-add-a-remote-http-server
- [definition] Option 2: Add a remote SSE server — The SSE (Server-Sent Events) transport is deprecated. Use HTTP servers instead, where available. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#option-2-add-a-remote-sse-server
- [definition] Option 3: Add a local stdio server — Stdio servers run as local processes on your machine. They're ideal for tools that need direct system access or custom scripts. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#option-3-add-a-local-stdio-server
- [definition] Option 4: Add a remote WebSocket server — WebSocket servers hold a persistent bidirectional connection, which suits remote MCP servers that push events to Claude unprompted. Use HTTP instead when your server only responds to requests, since HTTP supports OAuth and the `claude mcp add --transport` flag, while WebSocket supports neither. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#option-4-add-a-remote-websocket-server
- [definition] Add a server from setup instructions written for another client — MCP servers aren't specific to Claude Code, so a server's setup instructions may be written for Claude Desktop, Cursor, or another MCP client and give no `claude mcp add` command. To add the server anyway, look in those instructions for one of these three things: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#add-a-server-from-setup-instructions-written-for-another-client
- [definition] Managing your servers — Once configured, you can manage your MCP servers with these commands: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#managing-your-servers
- [definition] Disable a server without removing it — Toggle a server off in the `/mcp` panel to stop Claude Code from connecting to it without losing its configuration. Claude Code still lists the server in `/mcp`, marked as disabled. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#disable-a-server-without-removing-it
- [definition] MCP client runtimes — Claude Code connects to MCP servers through one of two client runtimes. The v1 runtime is built on MCP TypeScript SDK 1.x. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#mcp-client-runtimes
- [definition] Dynamic tool updates — Claude Code supports MCP `list_changed` notifications, allowing MCP servers to dynamically update their available tools, prompts, and resources without requiring you to disconnect and reconnect. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#dynamic-tool-updates
- [definition] Automatic reconnection — Claude Code reconnects a remote server that drops mid-session and retries an HTTP or SSE server's first connection after a transient error. Stdio servers are local processes, and Claude Code doesn't reconnect them automatically. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#automatic-reconnection
- [definition] Push messages with channels — An MCP server can also push messages directly into your session so Claude can react to external events like CI results, monitoring alerts, or chat messages. To enable this, your server declares the `claude/channel` capability and you opt it in with the `--channels` flag at startup. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#push-messages-with-channels
- [definition] Automatic backgrounding of long tool calls — An MCP tool call in the main conversation that is still running after two minutes moves to a background task instead of blocking the session. Claude receives the task ID immediately and keeps working, and the result arrives as a task notification when the call settles. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#automatic-backgrounding-of-long-tool-calls
- [definition] Plugin-provided MCP servers — [Plugins](/docs/en/plugins) can bundle MCP servers that provide tools and integrations when you enable the plugin. Plugin MCP servers work identically to user-configured servers. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#plugin-provided-mcp-servers
- [definition] MCP installation scopes — MCP servers can be configured at three scopes. The scope you choose controls which projects the server loads in and whether the configuration is shared with your team. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#mcp-installation-scopes
- [definition] Local scope — Local scope is the default. A local-scoped server loads only in the project where you added it and stays private to you. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#local-scope
- [definition] Project scope — Project-scoped servers enable team collaboration by storing configurations in a `.mcp.json` file at your project's root directory. When you add a project-scoped server, Claude Code automatically creates or updates this file with the appropriate configuration structure. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#project-scope
- [definition] User scope — User-scoped servers are stored in `~/.claude.json` and provide cross-project accessibility, making them available across all projects on your machine while remaining private to your user account. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#user-scope
- [definition] Scope hierarchy and precedence — When the same server is defined in more than one place, Claude Code connects to it once, using the definition from the highest-precedence source. The entire server entry from that source is used; fields are not merged across scopes. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#scope-hierarchy-and-precedence
- [definition] Environment variable expansion in `.mcp.json` — Claude Code supports environment variable expansion in `.mcp.json` files, allowing teams to share configurations while maintaining flexibility for machine-specific paths and sensitive values like API keys. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#environment-variable-expansion-in-mcpjson
- [definition] Example: Connect to GitHub for code reviews — GitHub's remote MCP server authenticates with a GitHub personal access token passed as a header. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#example-connect-to-github-for-code-reviews
- [definition] Example: Query your PostgreSQL database — [DBHub](https://github.com/bytebase/dbhub), the `@bytebase/dbhub` package, is an MCP server that connects Claude to a relational database through the connection string you pass in `--dsn`. Use a read-only database user in the connection string so the queries Claude runs can't modify data: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#example-query-your-postgresql-database
- [definition] Authenticate with remote MCP servers — Many cloud-based MCP servers require authentication. Claude Code supports OAuth 2.0 for secure connections. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#authenticate-with-remote-mcp-servers
- [definition] Add the server that requires authentication — If you already added the `sentry` server in the [MCP quickstart](/docs/en/mcp-quickstart#connect-a-server-that-requires-sign-in), skip this step: running `claude mcp add` again with the same server name at the same scope fails with `MCP server sentry already exists in local config`. Otherwise, run: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#authenticate-with-remote-mcp-servers
- [definition] Authenticate from the command line — From v2.1.186, `claude mcp login <name>` runs a configured server's OAuth flow directly from your shell, so you don't need to open the `/mcp` panel inside a session. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#authenticate-from-the-command-line
- [definition] Use a fixed OAuth callback port — Some MCP servers require a specific redirect URI registered in advance. By default, Claude Code picks a random available port for the OAuth callback. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#use-a-fixed-oauth-callback-port
- [definition] Use pre-configured OAuth credentials — Some MCP servers don't support automatic OAuth setup via Dynamic Client Registration. If you see an error like "Incompatible auth server: does not support dynamic client registration," the server requires pre-configured credentials. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#use-pre-configured-oauth-credentials
- [definition] Register an OAuth app with the server — Create an app through the server's developer portal and note your client ID and client secret. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#use-pre-configured-oauth-credentials
- [definition] Add the server with your credentials — Choose one of the following methods. The port used for `--callback-port` can be any available port. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#use-pre-configured-oauth-credentials
- [definition] Authenticate in Claude Code — Run `/mcp` in Claude Code and follow the browser login flow. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#use-pre-configured-oauth-credentials
- [definition] Override OAuth metadata discovery — Point Claude Code at a specific OAuth authorization server metadata URL to bypass the default discovery chain. Set `authServerMetadataUrl` when the MCP server's standard endpoints error, or when you want to route discovery through an internal proxy. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#override-oauth-metadata-discovery
- [definition] Restrict OAuth scopes — Set `oauth.scopes` to pin the scopes Claude Code requests during the authorization flow. This is the supported way to restrict an MCP server to a security-team-approved subset when the upstream authorization server advertises more scopes than you want to grant. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#restrict-oauth-scopes
- [definition] Use dynamic headers for custom authentication — If your MCP server uses an authentication scheme other than OAuth, such as Kerberos, short-lived tokens, or an internal SSO, use `headersHelper` to generate request headers at connection time. Claude Code runs the command and merges its output into the connection headers. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#use-dynamic-headers-for-custom-authentication
- [definition] Add MCP servers from JSON configuration — If you have a JSON configuration for an MCP server, you can add it directly: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#add-mcp-servers-from-json-configuration
- [definition] Import MCP servers from Claude Desktop — If you've already configured MCP servers in Claude Desktop, you can import them: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#import-mcp-servers-from-claude-desktop
- [definition] Select which servers to import — After running the command, you'll see an interactive dialog that allows you to select which servers you want to import. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#import-mcp-servers-from-claude-desktop
- [definition] Use MCP servers from claude.ai — If you've logged into Claude Code with a [claude.ai](https://claude.ai) account, MCP servers you've added in claude.ai, known as [connectors](https://claude.com/docs/connectors), are automatically available in Claude Code: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#use-mcp-servers-from-claudeai
- [definition] Configure MCP servers in claude.ai — Add servers at [claude.ai/customize/connectors](https://claude.ai/customize/connectors). On Team and Enterprise plans, only admins can add servers. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#use-mcp-servers-from-claudeai
- [definition] Authenticate the MCP server — Complete any required authentication steps in claude.ai. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#use-mcp-servers-from-claudeai
- [definition] How connectors reach Claude Code — Which settings govern a claude.ai connector depends on where your session runs, because only some sessions fetch connectors from claude.ai themselves. Each row below names how connectors arrive in one kind of session and what controls them there. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#how-connectors-reach-claude-code
- [definition] Organization controls on connector tools — Your organization can set per-tool controls on [claude.ai connectors](https://claude.com/docs/connectors). Claude Code reads these settings at startup and enforces them locally, except in the desktop app's [local and SSH sessions](#how-connectors-reach-claude-code). — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#organization-controls-on-connector-tools
- [definition] Disable claude.ai connectors — Claude Code applies [`disableClaudeAiConnectors`](/docs/en/settings-reference#disableclaudeaiconnectors) only to the connectors it [fetches itself](#how-connectors-reach-claude-code), not to the connectors a cloud host or the desktop app delivers. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#disable-claudeai-connectors
- [definition] Use Claude Code as an MCP server — You can use Claude Code itself as an MCP server that other applications can connect to: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#use-claude-code-as-an-mcp-server
- [definition] MCP output limits and warnings — When MCP tools produce large outputs, Claude Code helps manage the token usage to prevent overwhelming your conversation context: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#mcp-output-limits-and-warnings
- [definition] Raise the limit for a specific tool — If you're building an MCP server, you can allow individual tools to return results larger than the default persist-to-disk threshold by setting `_meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"]` in the tool's `tools/list` response entry. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#raise-the-limit-for-a-specific-tool
- [definition] Tool input schemas with a root-level combinator — Some MCP servers declare a tool's input schema as a JSON Schema union, with `anyOf`, `oneOf`, or `allOf` at the top level of the schema. The Claude API doesn't accept those keywords at the schema root. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#tool-input-schemas-with-a-root-level-combinator
- [definition] Tools with invalid input schemas — The Claude API checks every tool's input schema in a request and rejects the whole request when any one schema fails, so a single MCP tool with a malformed schema would make every request that includes it fail with a 400 error. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#tools-with-invalid-input-schemas
- [definition] Require approval for a specific tool — If you're building an MCP server, you can mark a tool as requiring explicit approval on every call by setting `_meta["anthropic/requiresUserInteraction"]` to `true` in the tool's `tools/list` response entry. The value must be the JSON boolean `true`; any other value is ignored. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#require-approval-for-a-specific-tool
- [definition] Respond to MCP elicitation requests — MCP servers can request structured input from you mid-task using elicitation. When a server needs information it can't get on its own, Claude Code displays an interactive dialog and passes your response back to the server. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#respond-to-mcp-elicitation-requests
- [definition] Use MCP resources — MCP servers can expose resources that you can reference using @ mentions, similar to how you reference files. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#use-mcp-resources
- [definition] List available resources — Type `@` in your prompt to see available resources from all connected MCP servers. Resources appear alongside files in the autocomplete menu. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#reference-mcp-resources
- [definition] Reference a specific resource — Use the format `@server:protocol://resource/path` to reference a resource: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#reference-mcp-resources
- [definition] Multiple resource references — You can reference multiple resources in a single prompt: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#reference-mcp-resources
- [definition] Scale with MCP tool search — Tool search keeps MCP context usage low by deferring tool definitions until Claude needs them. Only tool names and server instructions load at session start, so adding more MCP servers has minimal impact on your context window. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#scale-with-mcp-tool-search
- [definition] For MCP server authors — If you're building an MCP server, the server instructions field becomes more useful with tool search enabled. Server instructions help Claude understand when to search for your tools, similar to how [skills](/docs/en/skills) work. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#for-mcp-server-authors
- [definition] Configure tool search — Tool search is enabled by default: MCP tools are deferred and discovered on demand. Claude Code disables it when `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` points to a non-first-party host, since most proxies don't forward `tool_reference` blocks. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#configure-tool-search
- [definition] Exempt a server from deferral — If a server's tools should always be visible to Claude without a search step, set `alwaysLoad` to `true` in that server's configuration. Every tool from that server then loads into context at session start regardless of the `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH` setting. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#exempt-a-server-from-deferral
- [definition] Use MCP prompts as commands — MCP servers can expose prompts that become available as commands in Claude Code. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#use-mcp-prompts-as-commands
- [definition] Discover available prompts — Type `/` to see the commands available to you, including those from MCP servers. Claude Code lists each MCP prompt as `/servername:promptname (MCP)`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#execute-mcp-prompts
- [definition] Execute a prompt with arguments — Many prompts accept arguments. Pass them space-separated after the command. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#execute-mcp-prompts
- [definition] Managed MCP configuration — For organizations that need centralized control over which MCP servers users can connect to, see [Managed MCP configuration](/docs/en/managed-mcp). — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#managed-mcp-configuration

- [parameter] `! Connected · tools fetch failed`: The server connected but couldn't list its tools. Run `claude mcp get <name>` for the error detail — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart#add-and-verify-a-server
- [parameter] `! Needs authentication`: The server is reachable but needs a browser sign-in, or a token passed with `--header`. See [Connect a server that requires sign-in](#connect-a-server-that-requires-sign-in) — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart#add-and-verify-a-server

- [parameter] `✘ Connection error`: The connection attempt threw an error. See [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart#add-and-verify-a-server

- [definition] Where servers are saved — The `claude mcp add` command writes the server's details to a configuration file. By default it registers the server at `local` scope: private to you, active only in the current project. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart#where-servers-are-saved
- [definition] Find your configuration on disk — The `claude mcp add` command writes the server to one of three scopes, stored across two files, depending on the `--scope` flag. You don't need to edit these files directly, but knowing where they are helps with debugging and version control. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart#find-your-configuration-on-disk
- [definition] Change server scope — A server's scope is fixed when you add it, so changing scope means removing the entry and re-adding it at the new one. - [definition] Add a local server — A local stdio server is a program Claude Code starts as a subprocess on your machine, rather than a service it reaches over a URL. Use one for tools that need access to local resources like a browser, your filesystem, or a database socket. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart#add-a-local-server

- [definition] Use the browser — Give Claude a task that needs the browser: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart#add-a-local-server
- [definition] Connect a server that requires sign-in — Hosted services like Sentry, Linear, and Notion run their MCP servers behind OAuth: you add the server's URL, then sign in through your browser. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart#connect-a-server-that-requires-sign-in

- [definition] Use the server — Ask Claude something that needs the service, like `What Sentry projects do I have access to?`, and look for tool calls labeled with the `sentry` server name in its output. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart#connect-a-server-that-requires-sign-in
- [definition] Edit .mcp.json directly — Every file in the [scope table](#find-your-configuration-on-disk) uses the same JSON format for server entries. This section edits `.mcp.json`, the project-scope file. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart#edit-mcpjson-directly
- [definition] Connect from other surfaces — This guide uses the `claude mcp` CLI commands, but every Claude Code surface can connect to MCP servers: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart#connect-from-other-surfaces

- [definition] How Claude remembers your project — Give Claude persistent instructions with CLAUDE.md files, and let Claude accumulate learnings automatically with auto memory. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#how-claude-remembers-your-project
- [definition] CLAUDE.md vs auto memory — Claude Code has two complementary memory systems. Both are loaded at the start of every conversation. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#claudemd-vs-auto-memory
- [definition] CLAUDE.md files — CLAUDE.md files are markdown files that give Claude persistent instructions for a project, your personal workflow, or your entire organization. You write these files in plain text; Claude reads them at the start of every session. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#claudemd-files
- [definition] When to add to CLAUDE.md — Treat CLAUDE.md as the place you write down what you'd otherwise re-explain. Add to it when: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#when-to-add-to-claudemd
- [definition] Choose where to put CLAUDE.md files — CLAUDE.md files can live in several locations, each with a different scope. The table below lists them in load order, from broadest scope to most specific, so a project instruction appears in context after a user instruction. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#choose-where-to-put-claudemd-files
- [definition] Set up a project CLAUDE.md — A project CLAUDE.md can be stored in either `./CLAUDE.md` or `./.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Create this file and add instructions that apply to anyone working on the project: build and test commands, coding standards, architectural decisions, naming conventions, and common workflows. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#set-up-a-project-claudemd
- [definition] Write effective instructions — CLAUDE.md files are loaded into the context window at the start of every session, consuming tokens alongside your conversation. The [context window visualization](/docs/en/context-window) shows where CLAUDE.md loads relative to the rest of the startup context. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#write-effective-instructions
- [definition] Import additional files — CLAUDE.md files can import additional files using `@path/to/import` syntax. Imported files are expanded and loaded into context at launch alongside the CLAUDE.md that references them. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#import-additional-files
- [definition] AGENTS.md — Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md`, not `AGENTS.md`. If your repository already uses `AGENTS.md` for other coding agents, create a `CLAUDE.md` that imports it so both tools read the same instructions without duplicating them. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#agentsmd
- [definition] How CLAUDE.md files load — Claude Code loads `CLAUDE.md` and `CLAUDE.local.md` from your current working directory and every directory above it. Run Claude Code in `foo/bar/` and it loads instructions from `foo/bar/CLAUDE.md`, `foo/CLAUDE.md`, and any `CLAUDE.local.md` files alongside them. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#how-claudemd-files-load
- [definition] Organize rules with `.claude/rules/` — For larger projects, you can organize instructions into multiple files using the `.claude/rules/` directory. This keeps instructions modular and easier for teams to maintain. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#organize-rules-with-clauderules
- [definition] Manage CLAUDE.md for large teams — For organizations deploying Claude Code across teams, you can centralize instructions and control which CLAUDE.md files are loaded. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#manage-claudemd-for-large-teams
- [definition] Deploy with your configuration management system — Use MDM, Group Policy, Ansible, or similar tools to distribute the file across developer machines. See [managed settings](/docs/en/managed-settings) for other organization-wide configuration options. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#deploy-organization-wide-claudemd
- [definition] Auto memory — Auto memory lets Claude accumulate knowledge across sessions without you writing anything. As it works, Claude saves four kinds of notes for itself. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#auto-memory
- [definition] Enable or disable auto memory — Auto memory is on by default. To toggle it, open `/memory` in a session and use the auto memory toggle, which saves `autoMemoryEnabled` to your user settings at `~/.claude/settings.json`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#enable-or-disable-auto-memory
- [definition] Storage location — Each project gets its own memory directory at `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/`. The `<project>` path is derived from the git repository, so all worktrees and subdirectories within the same repo share one auto memory directory. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#storage-location
- [definition] How it works — The first 200 lines of `MEMORY.md`, or the first 25KB, whichever comes first, are loaded at the start of every conversation. Content beyond that threshold is not loaded at session start. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#how-it-works
- [definition] Audit and edit your memory — Auto memory files are plain markdown you can edit or delete at any time. Run [`/memory`](#view-and-edit-with-%2Fmemory) to browse and open memory files from within a session. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#audit-and-edit-your-memory
- [definition] View and edit with `/memory` — The `/memory` command lists your CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, and other memory file locations across user and project scopes, including user and project CLAUDE.md entries for files that don't exist yet. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#view-and-edit-with-memory
- [definition] Troubleshoot memory issues — These are the most common issues with CLAUDE.md and auto memory, along with steps to debug them. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#troubleshoot-memory-issues
- [definition] Claude isn't following my CLAUDE.md — CLAUDE.md content is delivered as a user message after the system prompt, not as part of the system prompt itself. Claude reads it and tries to follow it, but there's no guarantee of strict compliance, especially for vague or conflicting instructions. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#claude-isnt-following-my-claudemd
- [definition] I don't know what auto memory saved — Run `/memory` and select the auto memory folder to browse what Claude has saved. Everything is plain markdown you can read, edit, or delete. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#i-dont-know-what-auto-memory-saved
- [definition] My CLAUDE.md is too large — Files over 200 lines consume more context and may reduce adherence. Claude Code skips a file over 4 MiB. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#my-claudemd-is-too-large
- [definition] Instructions seem lost after `/compact` — Project-root CLAUDE.md survives compaction: after `/compact`, Claude re-reads it from disk and re-injects it into the session. Nested CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories and rules with [`paths:` frontmatter](#path-specific-rules) reload as Claude reads files they apply to. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#instructions-seem-lost-after-compact

- [definition] Work from your phone — From the app you can start cloud sessions, drive a Claude Code session running on your computer, or message Dispatch a task. The app is the same for all three; they differ in where the work happens. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mobile#work-from-your-phone
- [definition] Start and monitor cloud sessions — Claude Code on the web runs tasks on cloud infrastructure, Anthropic-managed by default, so a session continues after you put your phone away. From the Code tab, select a repository and branch, describe the task, and submit it. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mobile#start-and-monitor-cloud-sessions
- [definition] Continue a local session with Remote Control — Remote Control connects the Claude app to a Claude Code session running on your machine, so code execution and filesystem access stay local while you drive the session from your phone. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mobile#continue-a-local-session-with-remote-control
- [definition] Get push notifications — When Remote Control is active, Claude can send push notifications to your phone, typically when a long-running task finishes or when it needs a decision from you. You can also ask for one in your prompt, such as `notify me when the tests finish`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mobile#get-push-notifications
- [definition] Limitations — The mobile client covers most of what a session needs, with a few limitations: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mobile#limitations

- [definition] Administrator configuration — Administrators can configure OpenTelemetry settings for all users through the [managed settings file](/docs/en/managed-settings#delivery-mechanisms). See the [settings precedence](/docs/en/settings#settings-precedence) for more information about how settings are applied. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#administrator-configuration
- [definition] How managed settings lock the OTLP destination — When you set an `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_*` variable in managed settings, Claude Code removes conflicting developer-set variables at startup and logs a warning you can see with `claude --debug`. What it removes depends on which variable you set: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#how-managed-settings-lock-the-otlp-destination
- [definition] Common configuration variables — These variables configure exporters, endpoints, and export behavior for all deployments. If you set a per-signal endpoint or protocol variable, such as `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT`, Claude Code uses it instead of the generic variable for that signal. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#common-configuration-variables
- [definition] mTLS authentication — How you configure client certificates for the OTLP exporter depends on the OTLP protocol in use for that signal, set via `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL` or the per-signal override. The same configuration applies to metrics, logs, and traces. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#mtls-authentication
- [definition] Metrics cardinality control — The following environment variables control which attributes are included in metrics to manage cardinality: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#metrics-cardinality-control
- [definition] Traces (beta) — Distributed tracing exports spans that link each user prompt to the API requests and tool executions it triggers, so you can view a full request as a single trace in your tracing backend. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#traces-beta
- [definition] Dynamic headers — For enterprise environments that require dynamic authentication, you can configure a script to generate headers dynamically. Dynamic headers apply only to the `http/protobuf` and `http/json` protocols. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#dynamic-headers
- [definition] Multi-team organization support — Organizations with multiple teams or departments can add custom attributes to distinguish between different groups using the `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` environment variable: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#multi-team-organization-support
- [definition] Example configurations — Set these environment variables before running `claude`. Each scenario below shows a complete configuration, and each variable is described under [Common configuration variables](#common-configuration-variables). — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#example-configurations
- [definition] Standard attributes — All metrics and events share these standard attributes: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#standard-attributes
- [definition] Metrics — Claude Code exports the following metrics. The Unit column shows the OpenTelemetry unit string attached to each metric; count metrics carry none. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#metrics
- [definition] Metric details — Each metric includes the standard attributes listed above. Metrics with additional context-specific attributes are noted below. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#metric-details
- [definition] Events — Claude Code exports the following events via OpenTelemetry logs/events (when `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER` is configured): — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#events
- [definition] Interpret metrics and events data — The exported metrics and events support a range of analyses: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#interpret-metrics-and-events-data
- [definition] Cost monitoring — The `claude_code.cost.usage` metric helps with: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#cost-monitoring
- [definition] Detect retry exhaustion — Claude Code retries failed API requests internally and emits a single `claude_code.api_error` event only after it gives up, so the event itself is the terminal signal for that request. Intermediate retry attempts are not logged as separate events. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#detect-retry-exhaustion
- [definition] Event analysis — The event data describes each Claude Code interaction in detail: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#event-analysis
- [definition] Audit security events — OpenTelemetry events are the audit data source for Claude Code activity. Every event carries identity attributes that tie tool calls, MCP activity, and permission decisions back to the user who triggered them. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#audit-security-events
- [definition] Attribute actions to users — The [standard attributes](#standard-attributes) on each event include the authenticated user's identity: `user.email`, `user.account_uuid`, `user.account_id`, and `organization.id` when signed in with a Claude account, plus `user.id` and the per-session `session.id`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#attribute-actions-to-users
- [definition] Audit MCP activity — To capture MCP server activity with full call detail, enable the logs exporter and set `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1`. Each MCP operation then produces structured events that carry the server name, tool name, and call arguments alongside the standard identity attributes: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#audit-mcp-activity
- [definition] Map security questions to events — When building detection rules, look up the signal you want to monitor and query your backend for the corresponding event and attributes: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#map-security-questions-to-events
- [definition] Send events to a SIEM — Point `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_LOGS_ENDPOINT` at your SIEM's OTLP receiver, or at an OpenTelemetry Collector that forwards to your SIEM's native ingest API. The following managed-settings example exports events only, with full tool detail enabled for MCP and Bash auditing: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#send-events-to-a-siem
- [definition] Backend considerations — Your choice of metrics, logs, and traces backends determines the types of analyses you can perform: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#backend-considerations
- [definition] For traces — Choose a backend that supports distributed trace storage and span correlation: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#for-traces
- [definition] Service information — All metrics and events are exported with the following resource attributes: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#service-information
- [definition] ROI measurement resources — For a comprehensive guide on measuring return on investment for Claude Code, including telemetry setup, cost analysis, productivity metrics, and automated reporting, see the [Claude Code ROI Measurement Guide](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code-monitoring-guide). — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#roi-measurement-resources
- [definition] Monitor Claude Code on Amazon Bedrock — For detailed Claude Code usage monitoring guidance for Amazon Bedrock, see [Claude Code Monitoring Implementation (Amazon Bedrock)](https://github.com/aws-solutions-library-samples/guidance-for-claude-code-with-amazon-bedrock/blob/main/assets/docs/MONITORING.md). — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#monitor-claude-code-on-amazon-bedrock

- [parameter] `no-matching-tag`: Meaning=The dependency's repository has no `{name}--v*` tag satisfying the range.; How to resolve=Check that the upstream has tagged releases using the convention above, or relax your range. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-dependencies#resolve-dependency-errors

- [definition] How constraints interact — When several installed plugins constrain the same dependency, Claude Code intersects their ranges and resolves the dependency to the highest version that satisfies all of them. - [definition] Remove orphaned auto-installed dependencies — Auto-installed dependencies stay on disk after the plugins that installed them are uninstalled, in case you reinstall a dependent plugin or want to keep using the dependency directly. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-dependencies#remove-orphaned-auto-installed-dependencies

Create custom LSP plugins only when you need support for languages not already covered. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins#add-lsp-servers-to-your-plugin
- [definition] Add background monitors to your plugin — Background monitors let your plugin watch logs, files, or external status in the background and notify Claude as events arrive. ## How Claude Code uses prompt caching
<https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching>

- [parameter] System prompt: Content=Core instructions, tool definitions, output style; Changes when=The set of loaded tool definitions changes, or Claude Code is upgraded — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#how-the-cache-is-organized
- [parameter] Project context: Content=CLAUDE.md, auto memory, unscoped rules; Changes when=Session starts, or after `/clear` or `/compact` — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#how-the-cache-is-organized
- [parameter] Conversation: Content=Your messages, Claude's responses, tool results; Changes when=Every turn — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#how-the-cache-is-organized
- [parameter] Main conversation: Claude subscription, within plan usage=One hour; Usage credits, API key, or cloud provider=Five minutes — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#which-ttl-each-request-gets
- [parameter] Everything else: Claude subscription, within plan usage=Five minutes, except the server-controlled helper requests, which get one hour; Usage credits, API key, or cloud provider=Five minutes — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#which-ttl-each-request-gets
- [parameter] `cache_creation_input_tokens`: Tokens written to the cache on this turn, billed at the cache write rate — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#check-cache-performance
- [parameter] `cache_read_input_tokens`: Tokens served from cache on this turn, billed at roughly 10% of the standard input rate — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#check-cache-performance
- [parameter] `DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING`: Disable for all models — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#disable-prompt-caching
- [parameter] `DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_HAIKU`: Disable for Haiku only — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#disable-prompt-caching
- [parameter] `DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_SONNET`: Disable for Sonnet only — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#disable-prompt-caching
- [parameter] `DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_OPUS`: Disable for Opus only — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#disable-prompt-caching
- [parameter] `DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_FABLE`: Disable for Fable only — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#disable-prompt-caching
- [definition] How Claude Code uses prompt caching — Claude Code manages prompt caching automatically. See why a model switch triggers a slow uncached turn, what `/compact` costs, why CLAUDE.md edits don't apply mid-session, and how to check your cache hit rate. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#how-claude-code-uses-prompt-caching
- [definition] How the cache is organized — Each time you send a message in Claude Code, it makes a new API request. The model doesn't remember anything between requests, so Claude Code re-sends the full context: the system prompt, your project context, every prior message and tool result, and your new message. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#how-the-cache-is-organized
- [definition] Where the cache lives — Caching happens server-side, in whichever infrastructure serves your model. Where that is depends on how you authenticate: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#where-the-cache-lives
- [definition] Actions that invalidate the cache — These actions cause the next request to miss part or all of the cache. You see a one-time slower, more expensive turn, after which the new prefix is cached. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#actions-that-invalidate-the-cache
- [definition] Switching models — Each model has its own cache. Switching with [`/model`](/docs/en/model-config#setting-your-model) means the next request reads the entire conversation history with no cache hits, even though the content is identical. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#switching-models
- [definition] Changing effort level — The cache is keyed by [effort level](/docs/en/model-config#adjust-effort-level) as well as model, so switching with `/effort` means the next request reads the entire conversation history with no cache hits. Changing effort follows the same confirmation as [switching models](#switching-models). — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#changing-effort-level
- [definition] Turning on fast mode — Enabling [fast mode](/docs/en/fast-mode) adds a request header that is part of the cache key, so the first request Claude Code sends with fast mode on reads the entire conversation history with no cache hits. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#turning-on-fast-mode
- [definition] Connecting or disconnecting an MCP server — Tool definitions sit in the system prompt layer, so the cache invalidates when the set of tool definitions in the request changes between turns. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#connecting-or-disconnecting-an-mcp-server
- [definition] Enabling or disabling a plugin — When you enable or disable a [plugin](/docs/en/plugins), what the change costs depends on which component types the plugin provides. The cases below cover each component type, when Claude Code applies the change, and what happens when you disable a plugin again in the same session. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#enabling-or-disabling-a-plugin
- [definition] Denying an entire tool — Adding a bare tool name like `Bash` or `WebFetch` as a [deny rule](/docs/en/permissions#manage-permissions) removes that tool from Claude's context entirely. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#denying-an-entire-tool
- [definition] Compacting the conversation — [Compaction](/docs/en/context-window#what-survives-compaction) replaces your message history with a summary. By design, this invalidates the conversation layer, since the next request has a new, shorter history that doesn't share a prefix with the old one. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#compacting-the-conversation
- [definition] Upgrading Claude Code — A new Claude Code version typically updates the system prompt or tool definitions, so the first request after an upgrade rebuilds the cache from the top. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#upgrading-claude-code
- [definition] Actions that keep the cache — These actions either append to the end of the conversation or don't touch the request at all. Some of them, such as editing CLAUDE.md or changing output style, are also why a setting change waits for a restart to apply. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#actions-that-keep-the-cache
- [definition] Editing files in your repository — File contents enter context only when Claude reads them, and reads append to the conversation. Editing a file Claude previously read does not retroactively change the earlier read in history. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#editing-files-in-your-repository
- [definition] Editing CLAUDE.md mid-session — Your project-root and user-level CLAUDE.md files are read once at session start and held in memory. Editing them mid-session does not invalidate the cache, but the edit also doesn't apply. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#editing-claudemd-mid-session
- [definition] Changing output style — [Output style](/docs/en/output-styles) is part of the system prompt, which Claude Code reads once at session start. Changing it via `/config` or the `outputStyle` setting mid-session does not invalidate the cache, but the change also doesn't apply. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#changing-output-style
- [definition] Changing permission mode — Switching between [permission modes](/docs/en/permission-modes), such as from Manual to accept edits, does not change the system prompt or tool definitions, so mode changes are cache-safe. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#changing-permission-mode
- [definition] Invoking skills and commands — [Skills](/docs/en/skills) and [commands](/docs/en/commands) inject their instructions as user messages at the point of invocation. Nothing earlier in the conversation changes. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#invoking-skills-and-commands
- [definition] Running `/recap` — [`/recap`](/docs/en/interactive-mode#session-recap) generates a summary for display in your terminal. Unlike `/compact`, it appends the summary as command output rather than replacing your message history, so the cached prefix stays intact. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#running-recap
- [definition] Rewinding the conversation — [`/rewind`](/docs/en/checkpointing) truncates your conversation back to an earlier turn. The remaining history is the same content the cache was built from at that point, and the system prompt and project context layers are unchanged, so the next request hits the earlier cache entry. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#rewinding-the-conversation
- [definition] Cache lifetime — Cached prefixes expire after a period of inactivity. Each request that hits the cache resets the timer, so the cache stays warm as long as you keep working. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#cache-lifetime
- [definition] Which TTL each request gets — Claude Code decides the TTL per request, and every request falls in one of two fixed buckets: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#which-ttl-each-request-gets
- [definition] Choose the TTL yourself — You can set a TTL for either bucket. Each control takes `5m` or `1h`, and Claude Code ignores any other value. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#choose-the-ttl-yourself
- [definition] Cache scope — In Claude Code, the cache is effectively scoped to one machine and directory. The system prompt embeds the working directory, platform, shell, OS version, and auto memory paths, so two sessions in different directories build different prefixes and miss each other's cache. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#cache-scope
- [definition] Check cache performance — Cache performance shows up as two token counts the API reports on every response. The most direct way to watch them live is a [statusline script](/docs/en/statusline) that reads the `current_usage` object: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#check-cache-performance
- [definition] Subagents and the cache — A [subagent](/docs/en/sub-agents) starts its own conversation with its own system prompt and tool set, separate from the parent's. Its first request doesn't read the parent's cache, because the two prefixes differ, and it warms a cache of its own across its turns. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#subagents-and-the-cache
- [definition] Disable prompt caching — Disabling caching is occasionally useful when debugging caching behavior with a specific model or provider. To turn it off, set one of these environment variables to `1`: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching#disable-prompt-caching
