- [parameter] `/`: Meaning=Absolute path from filesystem root; Example=`/tmp/build` stays `/tmp/build` — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#configure-sandboxing
- [parameter] `~/`: Meaning=Relative to home directory; Example=`~/.kube` becomes `$HOME/.kube` — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#configure-sandboxing
- [parameter] `./` or no prefix: Meaning=Relative to the project root for project settings, or to `~/.claude` for user settings; Example=`./output` in `.claude/settings.json` resolves to `<project-root>/output` — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#configure-sandboxing
- [parameter] `"denyRead": ["~/"]` with `"allowRead": ["~/projects"]`: `~/projects` is readable and the rest of the home directory stays blocked. The narrower allow re-opens that part of the denied region — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#configure-sandboxing
- [parameter] `"allowRead": ["~/"]` with `"denyRead": ["~/.env"]`: `~/.env` stays blocked and the rest of the home directory is readable. The deny holds inside a wider allow, so a broad allow can't silently re-expose a secret — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#configure-sandboxing
- [parameter] `"allowRead": ["~/"]` with `"denyRead": ["~/**/.env"]`: Every `.env` under the home directory stays blocked and the rest is readable. A [wildcard deny](/docs/en/settings-reference#sandbox-path-prefixes) holds inside a wider allow the same way an exact path does — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#configure-sandboxing
- [parameter] `"mode": "deny"`: Pins `filesystem.disabled`=Yes; What protects the file when isolation is off=Nothing: the read block is part of the filesystem layer — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#which-settings-can-disable-it
- [parameter] `"mode": "mask"`, applied as a mask: Pins `filesystem.disabled`=No; What protects the file when isolation is off=Masking itself: the [sentinel copy and proxy](#mask-credential-files) on Linux and WSL2, the sandbox's own read rules on macOS — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#which-settings-can-disable-it
- [parameter] `"mode": "mask"`, [fallen back to `deny`](#mask-credential-files) at setup: Pins `filesystem.disabled`=No; What protects the file when isolation is off=Nothing, same as `deny`. List a path that can't be masked, such as a directory, as an explicit `deny` entry, which pins the key — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#which-settings-can-disable-it
- [parameter] `"mode": "mask"`, [degraded to `deny` by validation](/docs/en/managed-settings#invalid-entries-in-managed-settings): Pins `filesystem.disabled`=Yes, like an explicit `deny`; What protects the file when isolation is off=Nothing, same as `deny` — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#which-settings-can-disable-it
- [parameter] `filesystem.denyRead` and [`credentials.files`](#protect-credentials) `deny` read blocks: Not enforced. The filesystem layer applies both — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#what-changes-when-filesystem-isolation-is-off
- [parameter] `credentials.envVars` `deny` and `mask` entries: Enforced. Environment variable scrubbing is independent of the filesystem layer — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#what-changes-when-filesystem-isolation-is-off
- [parameter] [`credentials.files` `mask` entries](#mask-credential-files) applied as masks: Enforced: masking is independent of the filesystem layer. An entry that [fell back to `deny`](#mask-credential-files) is not enforced, like any `deny` entry — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#what-changes-when-filesystem-isolation-is-off
- [parameter] aws-chunked streaming uploads: `sigv4` key=`streaming`; Why the proxy can't re-sign it=Per-chunk signatures chain off the seed signature, so re-signing would require rewriting the body — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#re-sign-aws-requests
- [parameter] Presigned URLs: `sigv4` key=`presigned`; Why the proxy can't re-sign it=The signature lives in the URL itself, with no `Authorization` header — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#re-sign-aws-requests
- [parameter] SigV4A asymmetric signatures: `sigv4` key=`sigv4a`; Why the proxy can't re-sign it=There is no shared-key HMAC to recompute — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#re-sign-aws-requests
- [parameter] `sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite`: Grants subprocess write access to paths outside the working directory — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#permission-rules
- [parameter] `sandbox.filesystem.denyWrite` and `sandbox.filesystem.denyRead`: Block subprocess access to specific paths — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#permission-rules
- [parameter] `sandbox.filesystem.allowRead`: Re-allows reading specific paths within a `denyRead` region — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#permission-rules
- [parameter] [`sandbox.filesystem.disabled`](#disable-filesystem-isolation): Turns the filesystem layer off entirely while keeping network isolation — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#permission-rules
- [parameter] `Edit` allow rules: Grant write access to specific paths, the same way `sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite` does — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#permission-rules
- [parameter] `Read` and `Edit` deny rules: Block access to specific files or directories — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#permission-rules
- [parameter] `WebFetch(domain:...)` allow and deny rules: Control domain access — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#permission-rules
- [parameter] Sandbox `allowedDomains`: Controls which domains Bash commands can reach — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#permission-rules
- [parameter] Sandbox `deniedDomains`: Blocks specific domains even when a broader `allowedDomains` wildcard would otherwise permit them — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#permission-rules
- [parameter] `/sandbox`: What it controls=What a Bash command can access once it runs; What replaces the prompt=The sandbox boundary itself, in [auto-allow mode](#sandbox-modes) — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#permission-modes
- [parameter] [Auto mode](/docs/en/permission-modes#eliminate-prompts-with-auto-mode): What it controls=Whether each tool call runs; What replaces the prompt=A classifier that reviews actions — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#permission-modes
- [parameter] `--dangerously-skip-permissions`: What it controls=Whether each tool call runs; What replaces the prompt=Nothing. [Protected path](/docs/en/permission-modes#protected-paths) checks are also skipped; the [actions no mode auto-approves](/docs/en/permission-modes#actions-no-mode-auto-approves) still apply — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#permission-modes
- [definition] Configure the sandboxed Bash tool — Learn how Claude Code's sandboxed Bash tool provides filesystem and network isolation for safer, more autonomous agent execution. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#configure-the-sandboxed-bash-tool
- [definition] Get started — The sandbox is built into Claude Code and runs on macOS, Linux, and WSL2. Native Windows is not supported. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#get-started
- [definition] Run /sandbox — Start a Claude Code session and run the `/sandbox` command: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#get-started
- [definition] Choose a mode — On the Mode tab, select auto-allow or regular permissions. Auto-allow runs sandboxed commands without prompting, and regular permissions keeps the regular permission prompts even when commands are sandboxed. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#get-started
- [definition] Run a Bash command — Ask Claude to run a command, such as a build or a test suite. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#get-started
- [definition] Set up Linux and WSL2 — On Linux and WSL2, the sandbox relies on two packages: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#set-up-linux-and-wsl2
- [definition] Sandbox modes — Claude Code offers two sandbox modes. In both, the sandbox enforces the same filesystem and network restrictions; the difference is only in whether sandboxed commands are auto-approved or require explicit permission. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#sandbox-modes
- [definition] Configure sandboxing — Customize sandbox behavior through your `settings.json` file. See [Settings](/docs/en/settings-reference#sandbox-settings) for the complete configuration reference. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#configure-sandboxing
- [definition] Disable filesystem isolation — Set `sandbox.filesystem.disabled` to `true` to skip filesystem isolation while keeping network isolation. The example below turns off filesystem isolation while keeping an allowlist of network domains: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#disable-filesystem-isolation
- [definition] Protect credentials — The `sandbox.credentials` setting declares credential files and environment variables to protect from sandboxed commands. Each entry names a file path or an environment variable and a `mode`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#protect-credentials
- [definition] Mask credentials — Masking goes further than a `deny` entry under [Protect credentials](#protect-credentials). Instead of blocking a credential, Claude Code shows sandboxed commands a placeholder, the sentinel, and the [sandbox proxy](#network-isolation) swaps in the real value on outbound requests to hosts you allow. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#mask-credentials
- [definition] Filesystem isolation — The sandboxed Bash tool restricts file system access to specific directories: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#filesystem-isolation
- [definition] Protected paths — Inside the directories that sandboxed commands can write to, the sandbox still denies writes to the files Claude Code loads configuration and code from. A command that could edit those files could grant itself permissions, or add a hook or MCP server that Claude Code runs outside the sandbox. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#protected-paths
- [definition] Network isolation — Network access is controlled through a proxy server running outside the sandbox: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#network-isolation
- [definition] OS-level enforcement — The sandboxed Bash tool uses operating system security primitives: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#os-level-enforcement
- [definition] How sandboxing relates to permissions and permission modes — Sandboxing, [permission rules](/docs/en/permissions), and [permission modes](/docs/en/permission-modes) are complementary layers. The sections below cover how the sandbox interacts with each. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#how-sandboxing-relates-to-permissions-and-permission-modes
- [definition] Permission rules — Permission rules and sandboxing control different things: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#permission-rules
- [definition] Permission modes — `/sandbox` is not a [permission mode](/docs/en/permission-modes). Permission modes decide whether a tool call runs and whether you are prompted first, while the sandbox restricts what a Bash command can access once it runs. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#permission-modes
- [definition] Configure the sandbox for your organization — Administrators can require sandboxing for every user, keep developers from widening the policy, and route sandbox traffic through a corporate proxy. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#configure-the-sandbox-for-your-organization
- [definition] Enforce sandboxing with managed settings — To require the sandbox for every developer, deliver the `sandbox` keys through [managed settings](/docs/en/managed-settings#delivery-mechanisms), either as a file managed by your MDM or through [server-managed settings](/docs/en/server-managed-settings) on Claude.ai. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#enforce-sandboxing-with-managed-settings
- [definition] Keep developers from widening the policy — For boolean keys such as `enabled` and `failIfUnavailable`, Claude Code uses the managed value and ignores anything a developer sets locally. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#keep-developers-from-widening-the-policy
- [definition] Custom proxy configuration — For organizations requiring advanced network security, you can implement a custom proxy to: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#custom-proxy-configuration
- [definition] Troubleshooting — Some commands fail inside the sandbox even though they work outside it. The fixes below cover the most common cases. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#troubleshooting
- [definition] Limitations — Sandboxing reduces risk but is not a complete isolation boundary. Review the limitations below before relying on it as a hard security control. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#limitations
- [definition] Scope — The sandbox isolates Bash subprocesses. Other tools operate under different boundaries: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#scope

## Self-hosted environments
<https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments>

- [parameter] Environment: A named group of your runners, created in claude.ai settings. Sessions are routed to an environment, not to an individual runner. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments#key-concepts
- [parameter] Environment secret: The single shared credential runners use to authenticate and register with the environment. Shown once at environment creation, labeled **environment key** in the admin UI. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments#key-concepts
- [parameter] Runner: The long-lived process you deploy. A runner registers with the environment, receives a runner token, and polls for sessions. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments#key-concepts
- [parameter] Session: One Claude Code task, started from claude.ai, the mobile app, or another Anthropic surface such as a scheduled routine or an agent. Each session runs as a child Claude Code process the runner spawns. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments#key-concepts
- [definition] Self-hosted environments — Run Claude Code cloud sessions on infrastructure you control: set up a self-hosted environment, deploy runners, and route sessions to your own compute. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments#self-hosted-environments
- [definition] Why self-host — Most teams are better served by Anthropic-hosted environments, which need no infrastructure to run or maintain. Self-hosting is for teams whose network, tooling, or compliance requirements call for keeping session execution on infrastructure they control. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments#why-self-host
- [definition] Environments, runners, and sessions — Environments are managed on the **Cloud environments** page in claude.ai admin settings; runners are processes you start and manage on your own infrastructure. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments#environments-runners-and-sessions
- [definition] Key concepts — These terms appear throughout the self-hosted pages: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments#key-concepts
- [definition] Session lifecycle — When a developer starts a session and selects your environment, Anthropic's control plane places the session on the environment's queue. From there: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments#session-lifecycle
- [definition] Runner lifecycle — The first session a runner picks up locks the runner to that session's owner, and the runner runs up to `--capacity` concurrent sessions for that owner. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments#runner-lifecycle
- [definition] Network paths — The runner and its sessions make several kinds of outbound connection, and no inbound connectivity from Anthropic is required: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments#network-paths
- [definition] What stays on your infrastructure — Repository checkouts, build artifacts, secrets, and any files a session creates or modifies stay on the machines you provision. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments#what-stays-on-your-infrastructure
- [definition] Get started — The self-hosted environments pages are organized by what you're doing: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments#get-started

- [definition] Customize sessions in self-hosted environments — Customize self-hosted environment sessions with wrapper scripts for per-session credentials, lifecycle hooks, and on-demand runner spawning. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#customize-sessions-in-self-hosted-environments
- [definition] Wrapper scripts — Use a wrapper script when each session needs setup the runner can't do on its own: provisioning short-lived credentials scoped to the session creator, exporting environment-specific secrets, preparing language toolchains, or applying resource limits around the child process. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#wrapper-scripts
- [definition] Keep stdin and file descriptor 3 attached — The child's stdin is the runner's control channel. Token rotations and session-end signals arrive on it. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#keep-stdin-and-file-descriptor-3-attached
- [definition] Provision credentials scoped to the session creator — Use the `decode-token` subcommand to read claims from the session JWT. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#provision-credentials-scoped-to-the-session-creator
- [definition] Lifecycle hooks — Lifecycle hooks replace stages of the runner's per-session pipeline with your own scripts. Point the runner at a directory of hooks with `--hooks-dir <path>`, or `SELF_HOSTED_RUNNER_HOOKS_DIR`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#lifecycle-hooks
- [definition] checkout — Runs once per repository, in place of the runner's built-in clone and fetch. Use the hook to clone from a read-through mirror, seed a working tree from an archive, or apply per-session git auth. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#checkout
- [definition] post-session — Runs once per session, after the Claude Code child has exited and before the runner tears the workspace down. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#post-session
- [definition] command — Runs once per session after checkout, in place of the built-in child spawn. The hook receives the same environment as a [wrapper script](#wrapper-scripts) and should `exec` into `"$CLAUDE_RUNNER_CLAUDE_BIN"` the same way. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#command
- [definition] On-demand runners — Instead of running a fixed fleet, you can boot one runner per session. The orchestrator is a separate, stateless subcommand that polls Anthropic for spawn requests, one per session that's queued with no runner available, and runs your `spawn-runner` hook for each. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#on-demand-runners
- [definition] The spawn-runner hook — The orchestrator runs `${hooks-dir}/spawn-runner` once per spawn request. The hook must submit work asynchronously, without waiting for the runner to boot, and return within `--hook-timeout`, 60 seconds by default. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#the-spawn-runner-hook
- [definition] MCP servers — To make [MCP servers](/docs/en/mcp) available in every session, add them at image build time with the same `claude mcp add` command used on a desktop install. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#mcp-servers
- [definition] Prompt sessions to push their work — Anthropic-hosted sessions run a [`Stop` hook](/docs/en/hooks#stop), the Claude Code hook that runs when Claude finishes responding, that prompts Claude to commit and push its work. The runner doesn't install one. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#prompt-sessions-to-push-their-work
- [definition] Permissions and tool approval — A self-hosted session has no terminal attached, so an unanswered permission prompt stalls the turn until the user responds in the UI. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#permissions-and-tool-approval
- [definition] How each session's config is assembled — The runner gives each session its own config directory, seeded from an in-memory snapshot of the host's `~/.claude/` that the runner captures once at startup: `settings.json`, `CLAUDE.md`, hooks, agents, commands, and skills in your runner image apply to every session as the user-level baseline. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#how-each-sessions-config-is-assembled
- [definition] Repository-committed permission rules — Don't put a bare `"Edit"`, `"Write"`, or `"NotebookEdit"` entry in a repository-committed `permissions.allow`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#repository-committed-permission-rules

- [definition] Network requirements — The runner and the session children it spawns make outbound connections to the hosts below. - [definition] Default-deny egress — Deploy runner and session containers in a network segment or namespace whose outbound traffic is limited to the hosts in the [network requirements table](#network-requirements), your git host, and the specific internal services sessions need to reach. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-deploy#default-deny-egress

- [definition] Configure git — The runner manages repository checkouts but doesn't configure git identity or credentials by default. You control the runner's image and process environment, so you control the git config. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-deploy#configure-git

- [definition] Rewrite git URLs for private networks — Repository URLs arrive from the control plane as HTTPS, with the hostname of your git host; for GitHub Enterprise, that's the hostname you configured for the [GitHub Enterprise integration](/docs/en/github-enterprise-server) in Claude Code admin settings on claude.ai. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-deploy#rewrite-git-urls-for-private-networks
- [definition] Build the runner image — Anthropic doesn't publish a pre-built runner image. - [definition] Size CPU and memory for sessions — Size a runner's container or host for the sessions it runs rather than for the runner process. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-deploy#size-cpu-and-memory-for-sessions
- [definition] Kubernetes — The runner serves `GET /healthz` on port 8080 by default, configurable with `--health-port`, so Kubernetes probes work with no extra setup. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-deploy#kubernetes
- [definition] Docker Compose — The Compose service below restarts the runner whenever it exits, which covers both crashes and the normal exit after draining. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-deploy#docker-compose
- [definition] Shutdown timing — On `SIGTERM`, the runner stops taking new work and, unless you set [`--defer-shutdown-max-min`](#defer-the-drain-past-the-first-signal), waits up to `--drain-wait-sec`, zero by default, for in-flight turns to finish, terminates each session's process tree, and runs the [`post-session` lifecycle… — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-deploy#shutdown-timing

- [definition] What reaches a running post-session hook — The `post-session` hook and the Claude session child each run in their own POSIX process group, separate from the runner's, so stop mechanisms reach them differently: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-deploy#what-reaches-a-running-post-session-hook
- [definition] Keep the base directory and capacity identical across runners — If a runner dies mid-session, the server requeues the session and another runner in the environment picks it up. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-deploy#keep-the-base-directory-and-capacity-identical-across-runners
- [definition] Reuse a pre-warmed checkout — For large repositories, the clone can dominate session startup. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-deploy#reuse-a-pre-warmed-checkout
- [definition] Pin the version — Each session's child Claude Code process runs the runner's own binary, and the runner turns off auto-update inside the sessions it spawns, so every session runs the version you installed on the host or built into the image. - [definition] Scale the fleet — Your orchestrator decides when to add or remove runners. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-deploy#scale-the-fleet

- [definition] Some sessions don't count as idle — A session holding a background task that never finishes doesn't count as idle, so `--release-idle-session-min` won't release that session's slot. ## Verify session identity in self-hosted environments
<https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity>

- [snippet] Token format: sk-ant-cc-<base64url header>.<base64url payload>.<base64url signature> — `sk-ant-cc-<base64url header>.<base64url payload>.<base64url signature>` — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#token-format
- [snippet] Verify the token from your service: https://api.anthropic.com/v1/code/.well-known/jwks.json — `https://api.anthropic.com/v1/code/.well-known/jwks.json` — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#verify-the-token-from-your-service
- [snippet] Read the identity: import { createRemoteJWKSet, jwtVerify } from "jose"; — `import { createRemoteJWKSet, jwtVerify } from "jose";` — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#verify-the-token-from-your-service
- [snippet] Read the identity: import jwt — `import jwt` — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#verify-the-token-from-your-service
- [snippet] Verify the token inside the session: "$CLAUDE_RUNNER_CLAUDE_BIN" self-hosted-runner decode-token | jq -re '.act.attested_by.sub // .act.email // .act.sub' — `"$CLAUDE_RUNNER_CLAUDE_BIN" self-hosted-runner decode-token | jq -re '.act.attested_by.sub // .act.e` — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#verify-the-token-inside-the-session
- [parameter] `iss`: Type=string; Description=Always `ccr`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#claims-reference
- [parameter] `sub`: Type=string; Description=`ccr:session:<session_id>`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#claims-reference
- [parameter] `aud`: Type=array of strings; Description=Always contains `anthropic-api`. For sessions in self-hosted environments the array also contains your environment ID, such as `ccpool_...`. Verify the environment ID, not `anthropic-api`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#claims-reference
- [parameter] `exp`: Type=number; Description=Expiry as a Unix timestamp. Four-hour default lifetime, eight-hour maximum. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#claims-reference
- [parameter] `iat`: Type=number; Description=Issued-at as a Unix timestamp. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#claims-reference
- [parameter] `jti`: Type=string; Description=Unique token identifier. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#claims-reference
- [parameter] `ccr:role`: Type=string; Description=Always `session_worker` for session tokens. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#claims-reference
- [parameter] `ccr:session_id`: Type=string; Description=The session ID. Same value as the suffix of `sub`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#claims-reference
- [parameter] `ccr:pool_id`: Type=string; Description=Your environment ID. Same value that appears in `aud`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#claims-reference
- [parameter] `ccr:org_id`: Type=string; Description=Your Anthropic organization ID. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#claims-reference
- [parameter] `ccr:account_id`: Type=string; Description=The creating user's Anthropic account ID: the value of `act.sub` without the `user:` prefix, a tagged `user_...` ID. The same value the [spawn-runner hook](/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#the-spawn-runner-hook)'s `CLAUDE_RUNNER_ACCOUNT_ID` carries and [`--lock-to-account`](/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#runner-cli-flags)… — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#claims-reference
- [parameter] `account_email`: Type=string; Description=Duplicate of `act.email`; absent whenever `act.email` is. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#claims-reference
- [parameter] `organization_uuid`: Type=string; Description=Your Anthropic organization UUID. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#claims-reference
- [parameter] `account_uuid`: Type=string; Description=The creating user's Anthropic account UUID. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#claims-reference
- [parameter] `act`: Type=object; Description=[RFC 8693](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8693) delegation chain. See [The `act` chain](#the-act-chain). — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#claims-reference
- [parameter] `act.sub`: The creating user's Anthropic user ID, in the form `user:<id>`, or `agent:<id>` when your organization's service identity created the session, as it does for Claude Tag channel sessions. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#the-act-chain
- [parameter] `act.email`: The creating user's email address, when one was recorded at session creation. Don't require it; key on `act.sub`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#the-act-chain
- [parameter] `act.attested_by`: The upstream identity provider's attestation for the creating user, when available. `act.attested_by.sub` is the subject your SSO provider, such as Google or Okta, issued. Prefer this over `act.email` when mapping to identities in your own systems. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#the-act-chain
- [parameter] `act.act`: The runner that spawned the session. `act.act.sub` is `ccr:runner:<runner_id>`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#the-act-chain
- [parameter] `act.act.act`: The environment. `act.act.act.sub` is `ccr:pool:<pool_id>`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#the-act-chain
- [parameter] `act.act.act.act`: The identity that created the environment secret the runner registered with. The chain ends here. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#the-act-chain
- [definition] Verify session identity in self-hosted environments — Verify the CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ACCESS_TOKEN JWT so services on your network can trust requests from sessions in your self-hosted environment. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#verify-session-identity-in-self-hosted-environments
- [definition] The session token — Before you write verification code, know what the token establishes and the shape your JWT library will see. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#the-session-token
- [definition] What the token proves — A valid token establishes some facts and deliberately not others: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#what-the-token-proves
- [definition] Token format — The value of `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ACCESS_TOKEN` has an `sk-ant-cc-` prefix followed by a standard three-part JWT: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#token-format
- [definition] Verify the token — Verification runs in one of two places. Services on your network verify the token cryptographically against Anthropic's published keys, and wrapper scripts inside the session can use the runner binary's built-in decoder instead. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#verify-the-token
- [definition] Verify the token from your service — Anthropic publishes the verification keys at a public, unauthenticated endpoint: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#verify-the-token-from-your-service
- [definition] Check the prefix — Reject the value if it doesn't start with `sk-ant-cc-`, then remove that prefix. The remainder is a standard compact JWT. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#verify-the-token-from-your-service
- [definition] Verify the signature — Fetch the JWKS, select the key whose `kid` matches the token header, and verify the `ES256` signature. Reject tokens whose `alg` header is not `ES256`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#verify-the-token-from-your-service
- [definition] Verify the issuer — Reject the token if `iss` is not exactly `ccr`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#verify-the-token-from-your-service
- [definition] Verify the audience against your environment — The `aud` claim is an array. Reject the token unless it contains your environment ID, which has the form `ccpool_...`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#verify-the-token-from-your-service
- [definition] Verify the role — Reject the token if `ccr:role` is not exactly `session_worker`. Other tokens issued for self-hosted environments, such as environment secrets, runner tokens, and work orders, are signed by the same key set but carry different roles. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#verify-the-token-from-your-service
- [definition] Verify expiry — Reject the token if `exp` is in the past. Anthropic issues session tokens with a four-hour lifetime by default and a maximum of eight hours. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#verify-the-token-from-your-service
- [definition] Read the identity — The creating user's identity is in the `act` claim: `act.sub` is their Anthropic user ID in the prefixed form `user:<id>`, and `act.email`, when the creating surface recorded one, is their email address. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#verify-the-token-from-your-service
- [definition] Verify the token inside the session — [Wrapper scripts](/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#wrapper-scripts) run inside the session, before Claude starts. Instead of calling a JWT library, they can run the runner binary's `self-hosted-runner decode-token` subcommand. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#verify-the-token-inside-the-session
- [definition] Claims reference — The table below lists the session token claims relevant to verification. Read identity from the `ccr:*` namespace and the `act` chain; the flat `account_email`, `organization_uuid`, and `account_uuid` claims are backward-compatibility duplicates that may be removed. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#claims-reference
- [definition] The `act` chain — The `act` claim records the full delegation path from the user or service identity that created the session down to the [environment](/docs/en/self-hosted-environments#key-concepts) whose secret admitted the runner, and the identity that created that secret. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#the-act-chain
- [definition] Scope derived credentials — The session token identifies the user or service identity that created the session, but don't treat it as equivalent to that creator logging in directly. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#scope-derived-credentials
- [definition] Related environment variables — The creator identity also appears in plain environment variables on two surfaces that never verify the token: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-identity#related-environment-variables

- [definition] Set up an environment and runner — Claude Code includes a guided setup: an interactive Claude Code session that walks you through creating the environment in the admin UI, starts a local runner with the secret file you save, confirms that the runner registers, and writes a cheat sheet to `./runner-setup/CHEAT-SHEET.md`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-quickstart#set-up-an-environment-and-runner

- [definition] Start a runner — Create the secret directory. - [definition] Verify the runner appears — Return to the [**Cloud environments** page](https://claude.ai/admin-settings/cloud-environments). - [definition] Route a session to the environment — Start a session at claude.ai/code and select your environment from the environment picker, where self-hosted environments appear alongside Anthropic-hosted ones. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-quickstart#set-up-an-environment-and-runner
- [definition] Send a follow-up message to a running session — Once a session is running on your environment, send it a follow-up from the `claude` CLI on any machine where you're logged in with `claude auth login`; the command doesn't need to run from the machine that started the session. The command posts one message: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-quickstart#send-a-follow-up-message-to-a-running-session

- [parameter] `claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_pool_active_sessions`: Sessions currently assigned to an alive runner in this environment. Environment-wide aggregate, identical on every orchestrator instance: use `MAX` rather than `SUM` across instances. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#prometheus-metrics
- [parameter] `claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_spawn_hooks_total{result}`: Cumulative `spawn-runner` hook outcomes: `ok`, `retryable`, `non_retryable`. Counts orchestrator hook invocations, not session children the runners spawn: not comparable to `sessions_started_total`, since capacity above one, warm pools, and runners spawned again for the same session all diverge the two. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#prometheus-metrics
- [parameter] `claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_spawn_hook_duration_seconds`: Histogram of hook durations — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#prometheus-metrics
- [parameter] `claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_warm_hints_dispatched_total`: Standby spawn requests dispatched since process start — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#prometheus-metrics
- [parameter] `claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_session_queue_wait_seconds`: Histogram of seconds each session waited in the queue before the orchestrator claimed it for spawn, recorded from the queue-wait timestamp the control plane sends with each session's spawn request. Use for p50/p99 queue-time alerting. Pre-warming spawns aren't sampled. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#prometheus-metrics
- [parameter] `claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_clock_skew_seconds`: Local-minus-server clock skew; diagnostic, present once measured — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#prometheus-metrics
- [parameter] `claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_scm_connector_connected`: `1` when the [SCM connector](#scm-connector-flags)'s WebSocket is open; `0` while dialing or backing off. Absent when `--scm-connector-host` isn't set. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#prometheus-metrics
- [parameter] `claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_scm_connector_requests_forwarded_total`: Cumulative HTTP requests proxied to the configured SCM host since process start. Absent when `--scm-connector-host` isn't set. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#prometheus-metrics
- [parameter] Throughput: `claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_spawn_hooks_total{result="ok"}`, a counter on the long-lived orchestrator that increments once per successful `spawn-runner` hook and stays meaningful under `rate()`. It counts hook invocations rather than sessions, so pre-warming and repeated spawns for the same session diverge it from session counts. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#session-lifecycle-counter-semantics
- [parameter] Utilization: `sum(claude_code_self_hosted_runner_active_sessions)` against `sum(claude_code_self_hosted_runner_capacity)`, both gauges valid at every scrape regardless of runner lifetime — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#session-lifecycle-counter-semantics
- [parameter] Backlog: `claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_pool_pending_sessions` for queue depth, and `claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_queue_circuit_broken_sessions`, alerting if above zero — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#session-lifecycle-counter-semantics
- [parameter] Failures: `claude_code_self_hosted_runner_sessions_failed_total`, best effort: real crashes after spawn do increment it, and `rate()` is meaningful on runners that outlive their sessions with `--drain-grace-sec` above `0`. A one-shot environment has the same scrape-window problem as the other terminal counters, so treat any non-zero value you do see as worth investigating. Failures before spawn… — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#session-lifecycle-counter-semantics
- [definition] Self-hosted environments reference — Complete reference for the self-hosted runner and orchestrator: CLI flags, environment variables, and Prometheus metrics. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#self-hosted-environments-reference
- [definition] Runner CLI flags — Most flags have a corresponding environment variable. When both are set, the flag takes precedence. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#runner-cli-flags
- [definition] Orchestrator CLI flags — The `self-hosted-runner orchestrator` subcommand, which spawns [on-demand runners](/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration#on-demand-runners), accepts `--api-url`, `--environment-secret-file`, `--hooks-dir`, `--health-port`, and `--log-level` with the same defaults as the runner and, where… — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#orchestrator-cli-flags
- [definition] SCM connector flags — The orchestrator can hold a standing WebSocket connection to Anthropic's control plane so that hosted pre-session flows, such as the repository picker and the branch or ref resolver, can reach a GitHub Enterprise Server host that's only routable from inside your network. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#scm-connector-flags
- [definition] Environment-variable-only settings — These runner settings are read from the environment only and cover behavior most deployments leave at the default: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#environment-variable-only-settings
- [definition] Telemetry — Session children send operational telemetry to Anthropic unless you turn it off. No code or repository content is sent. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#telemetry
- [definition] Health endpoint — The runner serves `GET /healthz` on the configured health port. The response is `200 OK` whenever the process is alive, whatever state the poll loop is in, so an HTTP probe on this endpoint detects a dead process only. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#health-endpoint
- [definition] Prometheus metrics — Each runner serves Prometheus metrics at `GET /metrics` on the same port as `/healthz`. Key series: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#prometheus-metrics
- [definition] Pass through session-child metrics — Each session runs in its own child process with its own OpenTelemetry metrics; at `--capacity` above one, the runner rewrites how those child metrics are exposed. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#pass-through-session-child-metrics
- [definition] Session lifecycle counter semantics — The `sessions_started_total`, `sessions_completed_total`, `sessions_failed_total`, and `sessions_interrupted_total` counters classify each session by how it ended. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-reference#session-lifecycle-counter-semantics

- [definition] Settings precedence — When the same key appears in more than one place, Claude Code uses the value from the highest level that sets it. The stack below shows the levels, highest on top; a key at a higher level overrides the same key anywhere below it. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings#settings-precedence
- [definition] Lists merge instead of overriding — When you set the same list key, such as `permissions.allow`, in more than one file, Claude Code combines the lists instead of picking one, so each file can add entries without removing another file's. Three keys that hold model lists follow their own rules: — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings#lists-merge-instead-of-overriding

- [definition] Troubleshoot a setting that doesn't apply — When you set a key and Claude Code doesn't behave as if you had, start with `/status` to see which files it loaded, then find your symptom below. - [definition] Exceptions to managed settings precedence — For a few security-sensitive keys, Claude Code honors a restrictive value from a scope that otherwise couldn't override managed settings. - [parameter] Read from the highest-priority source only: How Claude Code combines it=Reads the key only from the highest-priority source that carries a policy key, so a lower source's value is ignored even when the highest source sets none; Keys=[`apiKeyHelper`](#apikeyhelper), [`awsAuthRefresh`](#awsauthrefresh), [`awsCredentialExport`](#awscredentialexport), [`gcpAuthRefresh`](#gcpauthrefresh)… — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#managedsourcesbehavior
- [parameter] `env`: How Claude Code combines it=[Merges per variable across admin sources](/docs/en/managed-settings#keys-read-from-every-admin-source), under both `"first-wins"` and `"merge"`; Keys=[`env`](#env) — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#managedsourcesbehavior
- [parameter] Every other key: How Claude Code combines it=Takes the value from the highest source that sets it; Keys=[`cleanupPeriodDays`](#cleanupperioddays), [`model`](#model) — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#managedsourcesbehavior

- [definition] Permission settings — Decide what Claude can do without asking, which permission mode a session starts in, and what auto mode's classifier allows. - [definition] `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` — Make managed settings the only source of `allow`, `ask`, and `deny` permission rules. By default, auto mode suspends only allow rules that could run arbitrary code: tool-wide and wildcard rules such as `Bash(*)`, and interpreter or shell-wrapper prefixes such as `Bash(python *)`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#automodeclassifyallshell

- [definition] `permissions` — Control which tools Claude can use without asking, which ones always prompt, and which ones are blocked, and set the [permission mode](/docs/en/permission-modes) a session starts in. - [definition] `useAutoModeDuringPlan` — Choose whether Claude Code uses the auto mode classifier to review shell commands in plan mode. With the default `true`, the classifier reviews each command during planning when auto mode is available and you see no prompt. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#useautomodeduringplan
- [definition] `permissions.allow` — List the tool uses Claude Code approves without asking you. In an MCP rule, `*` can appear only in the tool name after the `mcp__<server>__` prefix, such as `mcp__github__get_*`; it can't appear in the server name. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#permissionsallow
- [definition] `permissions.ask` — List the tool uses that prompt you for confirmation even in a permission mode that would otherwise approve them, such as `acceptEdits` or `bypassPermissions`. In `dontAsk` mode Claude Code denies a matching tool use instead of prompting. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#permissionsask
- [definition] `permissions.deny` — List the tool uses Claude Code blocks. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#permissionsdeny
- [definition] `permissions.additionalDirectories` — Give Claude file access to directories outside the one you started in, as additional [working directories](/docs/en/permissions#working-directories). — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#permissionsadditionaldirectories
- [definition] `permissions.defaultMode` — Set the [permission mode](/docs/en/permission-modes) new sessions start in. When you leave it unset, sessions start in the [built-in default](/docs/en/permission-modes#which-mode-a-session-starts-in) for your plan and surface. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#permissionsdefaultmode
- [definition] `permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode` — Prevent anyone from entering `bypassPermissions` mode. Claude Code then rejects the `--dangerously-skip-permissions` flag, and ignores an [agent definition's](/docs/en/sub-agents#permission-modes) `permissionMode: bypassPermissions`, so the subagent runs with the parent session's permission mode. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#permissionsdisablebypasspermissionsmode

- [definition] `skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt` — Skip the confirmation dialog Claude Code shows before a session enters `bypassPermissions` mode, whether from `--dangerously-skip-permissions` or from `defaultMode: "bypassPermissions"`. Claude Code writes `true` here in your user settings when you accept that dialog once. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#skipdangerousmodepermissionprompt
- [definition] Sandbox settings — Isolate the commands Claude runs from your filesystem, your network, and your credentials. For how sandboxing works and platform requirements, see [Sandboxing](/docs/en/sandboxing). — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandbox-settings
- [definition] `sandbox` — Isolate the Bash commands Claude runs from your filesystem and network with [sandboxing](/docs/en/sandboxing). Turn the sandbox on with `enabled`, then narrow or widen what sandboxed commands can touch with the `filesystem`, `network`, and `credentials` sub-objects. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandbox
- [definition] `sandbox.enabled` — Turn on [sandboxing](/docs/en/sandboxing) for Bash commands. When you pick a mode in the `/sandbox` panel, Claude Code writes this key to `.claude/settings.local.json` for the current project; set it in `~/.claude/settings.json` to sandbox every project. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxenabled
- [definition] `sandbox.failIfUnavailable` — Make Claude Code exit with an error at startup when `sandbox.enabled` is `true` but the sandbox can't start, because a dependency is missing or the platform is unsupported. Without it, Claude Code shows a warning and runs commands unsandboxed. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxfailifunavailable
- [definition] `sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed` — Let Claude Code run sandboxed Bash commands without a permission prompt. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxautoallowbashifsandboxed
- [definition] `sandbox.excludedCommands` — Name commands that Claude Code always runs outside the sandbox, such as tools that don't work under it. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxexcludedcommands
- [definition] `sandbox.allowUnsandboxedCommands` — Let Claude retry a command outside the sandbox with the `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` parameter after the sandbox blocks it. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxallowunsandboxedcommands
- [definition] `sandbox.filesystem` — Control which paths sandboxed commands can read and write. By default they can write to the working directory, any directories you add with `--add-dir`, and the session temp directory, and can read the rest of the filesystem, including credential files. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxfilesystem
- [definition] `sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite` — Add paths where sandboxed commands can write, beyond the working directory, the directories you've added with `--add-dir` or `/add-dir`, and the session temp directory. Use it when a subprocess such as `kubectl` or a build tool needs to write outside the project. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxfilesystemallowwrite
- [definition] `sandbox.filesystem.denyWrite` — Block sandboxed commands from writing to specific paths, including paths inside a directory that is otherwise writable. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxfilesystemdenywrite
- [definition] `sandbox.filesystem.denyRead` — Block sandboxed commands from reading specific paths, such as credential files that the default read policy would otherwise expose. To protect a credential file and keep it usable through the sandbox proxy, see [`sandbox.credentials`](#sandbox-credentials) instead. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxfilesystemdenyread
- [definition] `sandbox.filesystem.allowRead` — Re-open reading for specific paths inside a region that [`denyRead`](#sandbox-filesystem-denyread) blocks, to build workspace-only read access. An exact or wildcard `denyRead` entry stays blocked inside a broader `allowRead`, as the [overlap table](/docs/en/sandboxing#configure-sandboxing) shows. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxfilesystemallowread
- [definition] `sandbox.filesystem.allowManagedReadPathsOnly` — Honor only the [`allowRead`](#sandbox-filesystem-allowread) entries that come from managed settings, so developers can't re-open read access to paths your organization blocked. Claude Code still merges `denyRead` entries from every settings file the session loads. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxfilesystemallowmanagedreadpathsonly
- [definition] `sandbox.filesystem.disabled` — Skip filesystem isolation while keeping network isolation. Sandboxed commands get unrestricted read and write access to the host filesystem, and their network egress stays confined to [`network.allowedDomains`](#sandbox-network-alloweddomains). — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxfilesystemdisabled
- [definition] `sandbox.ignoreViolations` — Silence sandbox violation reports for paths you expect a command to probe and be refused, such as a tool that checks `/etc/hosts` on startup, so those denials don't show up as violations or in what Claude sees. The sandbox still blocks the access; only the report is suppressed. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxignoreviolations
- [definition] `sandbox.enableWeakerNestedSandbox` — Run the Linux sandbox inside an unprivileged Docker container, where bubblewrap can't mount a fresh `/proc`. Instead the inner sandbox bind-mounts the container's existing `/proc`, which exposes process information that a fresh mount would hide. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxenableweakernestedsandbox
- [definition] `sandbox.enableWeakerNetworkIsolation` — Let sandboxed commands on macOS reach the system TLS trust service, `com.apple.trustd.agent`. Go-based tools such as `gh`, `gcloud`, and `terraform` need it to verify TLS certificates when you use [`network.httpProxyPort`](#sandbox-network-httpproxyport) with a MITM proxy and a custom CA. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxenableweakernetworkisolation
- [definition] `sandbox.allowAppleEvents` — Let sandboxed commands on macOS send Apple Events, which `open`, `osascript`, and tools that open URLs in a browser need; without it they fail with error `-600`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxallowappleevents
- [definition] `sandbox.ripgrep` — Point the sandbox at a ripgrep binary of your own instead of the one Claude Code uses, for example when your platform needs a differently built `rg`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxripgrep
- [definition] `sandbox.bwrapPath` — Point the sandbox at a bubblewrap binary installed outside `PATH`, such as a vendored copy on an air-gapped host. Claude Code uses the path both for the startup dependency check and when it wraps each sandboxed command. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxbwrappath
- [definition] `sandbox.socatPath` — Point the sandbox network proxy at a `socat` binary installed outside `PATH`. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxsocatpath
- [definition] `sandbox.credentials` — Declare the credential files and environment variables to [protect from sandboxed commands](/docs/en/sandboxing#protect-credentials). — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxcredentials
- [definition] `sandbox.credentials.files` — Protect credential files or directories from sandboxed commands. With `"mode": "deny"`, Claude Code blocks reads of the path inside the sandbox, the same read block as [`sandbox.filesystem.denyRead`](#sandbox-filesystem-denyread). — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxcredentialsfiles
- [definition] `sandbox.credentials.envVars` — Protect environment variables from sandboxed commands. With `"mode": "deny"`, Claude Code removes the variable from the environment of sandboxed commands. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxcredentialsenvvars
- [definition] `sandbox.credentials.allowPlaintextInject` — Allow `mask` substitution on plain HTTP requests as well as TLS-terminated HTTPS. On plain HTTP the upstream identity is unverified and the credential travels in cleartext, so leave this off outside trusted test networks. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxcredentialsallowplaintextinject
- [definition] `sandbox.credentials.awsPairs` — Group masked environment variables that form one AWS credential for [SigV4 re-signing](/docs/en/sandboxing#re-sign-aws-requests) when your credential lives in variables with non-standard names. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxcredentialsawspairs
- [definition] `sandbox.credentials.sigv4` — Choose what the sandbox proxy does with AWS request forms it [can't re-sign](/docs/en/sandboxing#re-sign-aws-requests): `streaming` for aws-chunked streaming uploads, `presigned` for presigned URLs, and `sigv4a` for SigV4A asymmetric signatures. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxcredentialssigv4
- [definition] `sandbox.network` — Control which hosts, ports, and sockets sandboxed commands can reach. The sandbox routes outbound traffic through a proxy that enforces these lists; see [Network isolation](/docs/en/sandboxing#network-isolation) for how the proxy decides and when it prompts. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxnetwork
- [definition] `sandbox.network.allowUnixSockets` — List the Unix socket paths sandboxed commands can connect to on macOS. Claude Code ignores this list on Linux and WSL2, where the seccomp filter can't inspect socket paths; use [`allowAllUnixSockets`](#sandbox-network-allowallunixsockets) there instead. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxnetworkallowunixsockets
- [definition] `sandbox.network.allowAllUnixSockets` — Let sandboxed commands connect to every Unix socket. On Linux and WSL2, the sandbox's [seccomp filter](/docs/en/sandboxing#set-up-linux-and-wsl2) blocks `socket(AF_UNIX, ...)` calls, so this is the only way to permit Unix sockets there. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxnetworkallowallunixsockets
- [definition] `sandbox.network.allowLocalBinding` — Let sandboxed commands bind to localhost ports on macOS, for example to start a dev server. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxnetworkallowlocalbinding
- [definition] `sandbox.network.allowMachLookup` — List additional XPC and Mach service names the macOS sandbox may look up. Tools that communicate over XPC, such as the iOS Simulator or Playwright, need their services listed here. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxnetworkallowmachlookup
- [definition] `sandbox.network.allowedDomains` — Pre-allow domains for outbound traffic from sandboxed commands, so the sandbox doesn't prompt for them. Wildcards such as `*.example.com` match subdomains, and an optional `:port` suffix limits an entry to one port; an entry without a port matches every port. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxnetworkalloweddomains
- [definition] `sandbox.network.deniedDomains` — Block domains for outbound traffic from sandboxed commands, using the same wildcard, port, and IPv6 syntax as [`allowedDomains`](#sandbox-network-alloweddomains). A denied domain stays blocked even when an `allowedDomains` entry matches it too. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxnetworkdenieddomains
- [definition] `sandbox.network.strictAllowlist` — Deny sandboxed commands access to hosts outside the allowlist instead of prompting for approval. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxnetworkstrictallowlist
- [definition] `sandbox.network.allowManagedDomainsOnly` — Lock the network allowlist to what managed settings define. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxnetworkallowmanageddomainsonly
- [definition] `sandbox.network.httpProxyPort` — Point the sandbox at your own HTTP proxy instead of the one Claude Code runs. Organizations do this to inspect HTTPS traffic, apply their own filtering rules, or log every request. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxnetworkhttpproxyport
- [definition] `sandbox.network.socksProxyPort` — Point the sandbox at your own SOCKS5 proxy instead of the one Claude Code runs. When unset, Claude Code starts its own proxy for SOCKS traffic. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxnetworksocksproxyport
- [definition] `sandbox.network.tlsTerminate` — Make the sandbox proxy terminate TLS so it can read the contents of HTTPS requests. This is experimental, and `mask` [credential substitution](/docs/en/sandboxing#mask-credentials) requires it. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#sandboxnetworktlsterminate
